\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

\looseness=-1
We presented a cross-architecture representational analysis of instruction routing in vision-language-action models, studying three VLAs built on distinct backbone families across four LIBERO task suites.
Our three complementary analyses---layer-wise action probing, counterfactual instruction perturbation, and L1 attention profiling---consistently decompose VLA instruction routing into two distinct patterns: training-associated effects and inherited base-model priors.
Exit collapse ($\Delta R^2 = 0.16$--$0.46$) and graded counterfactual sensitivity ($d = 0.45$--$1.52$) emerge specifically from VLM-to-VLA fine-tuning---absent in both VLA-to-VLA and NLP-only controls---while L1 attention routing is inherited from reference backbones.
These findings enable practical diagnostics: $\Delta R^2 > 0.10$ flags under-utilized exit-layer representations without rollouts, and mid-layer features offer principled tap points for downstream reward models and planners.
The cross-architecture consistency suggests these are general properties of autoregressive VLA fine-tuning, not artifacts of any single model design.

\section{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

\looseness=-1
Our conclusions rest on $N{=}2$ VLM-to-VLA transitions plus one VLA-to-VLA case, all autoregressive decoders evaluated on a single benchmark (LIBERO); flow-matching~\cite{black2024_pi0} and diffusion~\cite{ghosh2024_octo} action heads may behave differently.
All findings are correlational---$R^2$ measures decodability, not causal reliance---and evaluations are open-loop; the $\Delta R^2$--success-rate correlation ($\rho{=}0.583$, $p{=}0.10$; Appendix~\ref{sec:extended_discussion_appendix}) is suggestive but underpowered ($n{=}9$).
Extending to additional architectures, non-autoregressive action heads, and closed-loop behavioral validation are priorities for future work.
